look_here_first: Look for the comparatively DENSE panicle: large, many-flowered spikelets packed into clusters along ascending branches. Many can appear rosy-red or violet, but spikelet DENSITY and CLUSTERING are stronger than color. Use a mature isolated spikelet to confirm multiple florets before deciding.

project_inclusion.range_basis: Hays, Blanco, and Llano — specimen-backed county records in Hagenbuch & Lemke's Texas Hill Country grass treatment.

best_field_traits: leaf blades narrow, flat to involute
spikelets conspicuously clumped along branches and branchlets
spikelets pale green to violet or reddish
branch angle appressed to ascending rather than broadly divergent
morphology_keys.comparison_training: The clustered, reddish spikelets are the fast cue. E. spectabilis has many widely spaced spikelets on flexuous, broadly spreading branches; E. lugens has a more restrained panicle and very narrow involute leaves.
morphology_keys.field_teaching_note: Kew/GrassBase describes secundiflora with spikelets clumped along branches, typically many-flowered, 6–20 mm in broader treatment. The photo labels mark clusters only: there are no counted, measured florets.

comparisons.key_distinctions: E. spectabilis: open flexible cloud with more separate spikelets; E. cilianensis: annual often with conspicuous craterlike glands along branchlets and lemma keels. E. lugens: narrow inrolled leaves and markedly smaller solitary spikelets; Tridens texanus: do not assume genus from reddish panicle, verify grass spikelet floral details.

field_photo_quickcheck.heading: Eragrostis secundiflora — follow the real-photo field cues
steps: START with the USGS inflorescence image: follow a PRIMARY PANICLE BRANCH, then identify several separate, crowded, many-flowered SPIKELETS. The spikelets are not individual seeds.
COMPARE the existing reddish and dried head photographs: clustered spikelets remain the useful character after red pigment fades; color by itself is not identification.

FIND the leaf BLADE-SHEATH JUNCTION on a fresh specimen and focus at 10–20×. Photograph the very short ciliate/hair-fringed ligule, separately from the longer hairs that may occur at the top (mouth) of the sheath; do not label sheath-mouth hairs as the ligule.

PHOTOGRAPH one intact flattened mature spikelet against a 1-mm ruler, then a carefully separated lower and upper glume, individual lemma and palea. Count attached florets only where clear; published counts are not measurements of these photos.

PLACE a matched E. spectabilis panicle beside it at the same scale and maturity. Red lovegrass tends to crowd several chunkier spikelets together; purple lovegrass has a more openly spreading, airy flowering structure.

Check the stems and lower sheath on a rooted plant and compare the glandular characters of E. cilianensis where present. If anatomy is not resolvable, retain Eragrostis sp. rather than inferring species from color or height.
field_photo_quickcheck.field_rule: Teach CLUSTERS on the branching panicle first; confirm separate flattened many-flowered SPIKELETS and the actual tiny blade-sheath ligule (not longer sheath-mouth hairs) with a 1-mm scale. E. spectabilis is comparatively airy and spread out.
field_photo_quickcheck.warning: Existing USGS photos show clustered inflorescence architecture; the two archived library photographs are provisional broad views. No existing record certifies sheath-mouth hair insertion, ligule macro, glume/lemma separation, or a measured floret count. Do not make arrows to these invisible organs. The third remote derivative image remains publication-rights-review, not a verified archive.
